source.title: Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality
source.authors: Wenhao Wu; Yizhong Wang; Guang-Xuan Xiao; Hao Peng; Yao Fu

page_placements.theme: Post-pretraining training preserves or strengthens induction and retrieval heads
Retrieval heads in long-context retrieval, many-shot ICL and grounded generation

record.tranche_reason: The study measures and intervenes on retrieval heads for long-context information retrieval. It cites induction heads as motivation and explicitly distinguishes the two, but does not test the induction-head claims or their predicted training and in-context-learning behavior.
record.gate_note: The study reports results about retrieval heads, a related but distinct mechanism: it says they redirect information according to context but do not infer programs. It does not measure induction-head formation, loss changes over training, or in-context learning as defined in the claim. Retrieval-head findings are recorded as none-version results.
record.test_reason: The study detects and masks retrieval heads, which copy needle tokens in long-context retrieval, in 7B–34B LLMs. It cites induction heads only as inspiration and contrasts the two in its Discussion. It measures no prefix-matching or [A][B]…[A]→[B] behaviour, no previous-token composition, no training dynamics and no loss-by-token in-context learning. Retrieval-head findings are a related but different construct, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that retrieval heads are a sparse, universal, intrinsic and causal set of heads implementing conditional copy, which explains long-context factuality and also affects CoT. They say induction heads search repeated patterns, whereas retrieval heads redirect information by context and do not infer programs.
record.recipe_differences: The study detects retrieval heads using token-level copy-paste scores on Needle-in-a-Haystack tests and tests them by masking. It does not use the induction-head training analysis or measure in-context learning from the original work.
record.method_sensitivity: Retrieval-head activation varies with context and token; downstream masking effects differ between CoT and answer-only prompting. The paper also varies the number of masked heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse retrieval heads (about 3–6% of heads with score >0.1) exist in all studied long-context LLM families and scales.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Long-context LLMs across families contain a sparse set of attention heads that copy needle tokens from context to output.

fits_no_version.finding: Retrieval-head patterns are preserved from base models to continued-pretrained, chat and upcycled variants (r>0.8) but differ across families (r<0.1). Some heads activate in all tested contexts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Retrieval heads arise in pretraining and are reused by derived models.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking retrieval heads harms NIAH, extractive QA and CoT performance; random-head masking and answer-only prompting are largely unaffected.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Retrieval heads causally support long-context factual retrieval and CoT that refers back to the input.

record.problems: The experiments measure retrieval heads, not induction heads or in-context learning as defined in the claim. No training trajectory or loss-curve analysis is reported. Some plotted values are not clearly assignable from the flattened figure text, and uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results about induction heads or the versions in the claim were reported. Some numerical values in Figures 7, 8, and 10 were not separately extracted where the flattened text did not securely map them to conditions.

untested.parts: Induction-head composition with previous-token heads and the [A][B]…[A]→[B] behaviour; not measured.
Training-time onset, abruptness, loss bump and co-occurring in-context-learning gain; no training trajectories.
Induction heads' share of loss-by-token in-context learning in large models; not measured.
Presence of induction heads across families, sizes or architectures. Only retrieval heads were surveyed.
Effect of data or training setup on induction-head formation or persistence of in-context learning; not measured.
Which heads carry few-shot task learning; not measured.
Sub-steps of induction-head formation; not measured.

record.verdict_notes: Retrieval-score detection resembles copying behaviour but is not prefix-matching induction, so no row bears on any version. It might be argued the study is relevant to V4-style universality of copying heads, but no induction metric is computed. The NIAH result with all heads masked at K=50 (below 50 for all models) is in the text but concerns retrieval heads only.

versions.untested_parts: Induction-head composition with previous-token heads and the [A][B] … [A] → [B] behavior.
Training-time onset, abruptness, loss-curve bump, and temporal relation to in-context-learning gains.
Whether induction heads explain most loss-by-token in-context learning in large transformers.
Universality of induction behavior across models, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Effects of training data and setup on induction-head formation or persistence of in-context learning.
Whether few-shot task learning is mainly carried by mechanisms other than induction heads.
Whether induction-head formation comprises multiple sub-steps or overlapping transitions.

relation.reason: The introduction draws inspiration from induction heads, and Section 5 explicitly compares their function with retrieval heads. Induction heads are neither experimentally tested nor used as an operational tool.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure conditional retrieval and copying, a related but different construct. They do not test induction behavior, previous-token composition, training transitions, or induction heads' contribution to in-context or few-shot learning.

source_check.notes: Section 3.2 and the abstract support 12 always-active Llama retrieval heads; the introduction instead says 13. Section 4.2 explicitly reports 9.2% and 23.1% F1 reductions, but Figure 8 gives 56.7, 47.5 and 32.3, implying decreases of 9.2 and 24.4 F1 points.

statements.correction: Retrieval heads comprise about 3–6% of heads at retrieval score >0.1 across studied models. Retrieval-head masking harms NIAH, extractive QA and CoT. Random-head masking has a much weaker impact on NIAH and no significant impact on extractive QA; CoT performance can also decline under random-head masking.
statements.problem: The assertion that random-head masking does not harm performance is too broad: Section 4.1 reports a smaller impact on NIAH, and Figure 10 shows CoT performance can decline with random-head masking.
